title: Procédure de déploiement en production (v2)
content:
## Contexte

Depuis la migration vers le pipeline v2, Coralis Desk se déploie par tag Git
signé, jamais depuis une branche. Cette note remplace toutes les procédures
antérieures à mars 2026 et sert de référence pour l'astreinte.

## Prérequis

- Accès au bastion de production (clé SSH personnelle, pas de clé partagée).
- Être membre du groupe `deploy-prod` dans l'annuaire interne.
- Avoir vérifié que la CI est verte sur `main` (GitHub Actions, workflow
  `release.yml`).
- Prévenir sur le canal Slack `#déploiements` au moins quinze minutes avant.

## Étapes de déploiement

### 1. Préparation

Créer le tag de version en suivant le semver (`v2.14.3` par exemple), puis
le pousser. Le pipeline construit les images Docker et les publie dans le
registre interne.

### 2. Fenêtre de gel

Aucun déploiement n'est autorisé le vendredi après 16h, sauf correctif de
sécurité critique validé par le responsable ops. La variable d'environnement
`DEPLOY_FREEZE_WINDOW_HOURS` fixe la durée du gel du week-end (48h par
défaut) et bloqué le pipeline si on tente de forcer un déploiement pendant
cette fenêtre.

### 3. Déploiement progressif

Le trafic est basculé par vagues de 10%, 50%, puis 100%, avec dix minutes
d'observation entre chaque palier. Le tableau de bord de latence et de taux
d'erreur doit rester stable avant de passer au palier suivant.

## Que faire si on doit déployer un vendredi soir

C'est la question qui revient le plus souvent en astreinte. La réponse
courte : on ne le fait pas, sauf incident de sécurité actif. Si c'est
vraiment nécessaire, il faut l'accord explicite du responsable ops par
écrit (message Slack suffit), et un déploiement hors gel doit systématiquement
être suivi d'une astreinte renforcée jusqu'au lundi matin. Dans les faits,
la quasi-totalite des demandes de déploiement du vendredi soir sont refusées
et reportées au lundi.

## Rollback

```bash
# revenir à la version précédente en moins de deux minutes
./deploy.sh rollback --to=previous
# vérifier que le trafic est revenu sur l'ancienne version
./deploy.sh status
```

Si le rollback automatique échoué, contacter directement le responsable ops
via l'astreinte téléphonique, ne pas attendre la réponse Slack.

## Historique

Cette procédure a remplacé l'ancienne procédure de déploiement manuel
(voir la note correspondante, marquée obsolète) le jour où le pipeline v2
est passe en production pour tout le monde.

## Astreinte et escalade

La personne d'astreinte n'est pas forcément celle qui a fait le
déploiement. Le planning d'astreinte tourne par semaine, indépendamment du
calendrier des déploiements, et il est affiché sur le canal Slack
`#astreinte`. Si un problème survient pendant ou juste après un
déploiement, la personne d'astreinte est prévenue en priorité, même si elle
n'a pas participé au déploiement lui-même.

En cas de doute sur la gravité d'un problème post-déploiement, la règle est
simple : on considère que c'est grave jusqu'à preuve du contraire, on ne
laisse jamais une anomalie "pour voir si ca se confirme" pendant plus de
quelques minutes sans agir.

## Vérifications post-déploiement

Une fois le palier de 100% atteint, une checklist courte doit être suivie
avant de considérer le déploiement terminé :

- Les tests de fumée automatiques (login, création de ticket, changement de
  statut) passent sur l'environnement de production.
- Aucune augmentation anormale du taux d'erreur côté API sur les quinze
  dernières minutes.
- Le webhook de facturation (intégration PayLoop) reçoit et traite
  correctement au moins un événement de test si le déploiement touchait au
  code de facturation.
- Les migrations de base de données associées, si elles existent, sont
  bien passées à `applied` dans le suivi des migrations, pas seulement
  exécutées sans erreur visible dans les logs.

## Communication après un déploiement qui a mal tourné

Si un rollback a été nécessaire, un message récapitulatif est posté sur
`#déploiements` avec : ce qui a été déployé, ce qui a cassé, l'heure du
rollback, et si un ticket de suivi (correction ou postmortem) a été ouvert.
Ce message n'attend pas le postmortem complet, qui peut arriver plusieurs
jours plus tard ; il sert à informer l'équipe rapidement, dans les minutes
qui suivent le rollback.

## Cas particulier : déploiement lié à un correctif de sécurité

Un correctif de sécurité critique peut déroger à la fenêtre de gel du
vendredi soir mentionnée plus haut, mais uniquement si le responsable ops
donné son accord explicite. Dans ce cas, l'astreinte reste mobilisée toute
la nuit et le lendemain matin, même si le déploiement s'est bien passe en
apparence, par précaution.

title: Ancienne procédure de déploiement (abandonnée)
content:
Avant la mise en place du pipeline v2, le déploiement de Coralis Desk se faisait à la main depuis le posté du responsable ops : on se connectait en
SSH sur chaque serveur applicatif, on tirait la dernière version depuis
`main`, on relançait le service avec `systemctl restart coralis-api`, puis
on vérifiait à l'œil les logs pendant cinq minutes.

Cette méthode n'avait aucune notion de fenêtre de gel, aucun rollback
automatique, et dépendait entièrement de la mémoire de la personne qui
déployait pour savoir dans quel ordre relancer les services. Elle a
provoqué au moins deux incidents de production documentés en 2025, dont un lié à un oubli de migration de base de données avant redémarrage.

Cette procédure est abandonnée depuis le passage au pipeline v2 et ne doit
plus être suivie. Elle reste documentée ici uniquement pour comprendre les
tickets d'incident anciens qui y font référence.

title: Politique de congés - équipe France
content:
La politique de congés pour l'équipe basée en France suit le cadre legal
standard : 25 jours de congés payés par an plus les RTT accordées selon le
nombre de jours travailles. Les demandes de congés se font via le formulaire
RH interne, avec un délai de prévenance recommandé de deux semaines pour les
absences de plus de trois jours.

Aucune demande n'est validée automatiquement pendant les périodes de forte
charge (lancement produit, clôture comptable de fin d'année). En cas de
congés maladie, un justificatif doit être transmis dans les 48h à la personne en charge des RH.

Les jours fériés suivent le calendrier officiel français (voir la note
dédiée au calendrier des jours fériés). Les congés non pris ne sont pas
reportables au-dela du 31 mars de l'année suivante, sauf accord écrit
exceptionnel.

title: 休假政策-中国办公室
content:
中国办公室的休假政策遵循国家法定标准并结合公司内部规定。员工每年享有五天年假,工作满三年后每年增加一天,最多累计到十五天。请假需要提前至少三个工作日通过内部系统提交申请,超过五天的连续休假需要提前两周申请并获得直属负责人书面同意。

病假需要在请假当天上午通知直属负责人,并在返岗后三天内提交医院开具的证明。产假、陪产假按照当地劳动法规执行,具体天数由人事负责人在入职时说明,不在本文档中重复列出。

年假不可跨自然年结转,唯一例外是因公司业务原因导致员工无法休完当年年假,需由部门负责人书面确认后方可延期至次年三月底之前使用。法定节假日安排见另一份专门的节假日日历文档,与本政策相互独立,不要混用两份文档中的天数。

title: Postmortem: August billing webhook outage
content:
## Summary

On August 19th, Coralis Desk stopped processing incoming billing webhooks
from our payment vendor PayLoop for roughly 47 minutes. No customer data
was lost, but around 300 invoices were marked as pending instead of paid
until the backlog was replayed.

## Timeline

- 14:02 UTC - Alert fires in Slack `#alerts-prod`: webhook queue depth above
  threshold.
- 14:06 UTC - On-call engineer acknowledges, starts investigating the
  webhook consumer service.
- 14:21 UTC - Root cause identified: the deploy earlier that day rotated
  the value behind `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME` without updating the
  vendor-side signing secret first, so every incoming request failed
  signature verification and was dropped silently.
- 14:35 UTC - Fix rolled out: secret rotation reverted, vendor notified.
- 14:49 UTC - Queue confirmed draining, webhook processing back to normal.

## Root cause

The runbook for rotating `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME` did not enforce the
order of operations (update vendor first, then our side). The engineer who
rotated it followed the general secret-rotation checklist, which is correct
for most secrets but wrong for a shared webhook signing secret.

## Why this went unnoticed for so long

Nothing in the deploy pipeline validated that webhook signature checks were
still succeeding after a secret rotation. The monitoring only alerted on
queue depth, which took several minutes to cross the threshold.

## Customer impact

Around 300 invoices briefly showed as "pending" in the dashboard instead of
"paid". No payment was actually lost or duplicated; the webhook replay from
PayLoop's side caught up automatically once signature verification passed
again.

## Follow-up actions

1. Add a synthetic webhook check that fires every five minutes and pages if
   signature verification fails twice in a row.
2. Update the secret-rotation runbook to call out shared-secret rotations
   (billing webhook, but also the support-ticket import webhook) as a
   special case requiring vendor coordination.
3. Reduce the alert threshold on webhook queue depth so we notice within
   two minutes instead of four.

This incident is unrelated to the earlier outage discussed in the March
postmortem, which had a completely different root cause (database
connection pool exhaustion), even though both produced a similar symptom of
invoices stuck in "pending" state.

## Detailed impact breakdown

Of the roughly 300 affected invoices, about 260 belonged to workspaces on
the Team tier, and the remaining 40 to Scale-tier workspaces with heavier
API usage. No Starter-tier workspace was affected, most likely because
Starter workspaces generate invoices less frequently and none happened to
fall in the affected window by chance.

## Why the on-call engineer's first hypothesis was wrong

The on-call engineer initially suspected a PayLoop-side outage, since the
symptom (webhooks stopping) looked identical to a vendor incident. Fifteen
minutes were spent checking PayLoop's public status page and posting in
their support channel before the secret rotation was even considered as a
cause. This delay is called out explicitly in the follow-up actions below,
because the deploy log that would have pointed at the rotation immediately
was not checked first.

## Follow-up actions (continued)

4. Add a note to the on-call runbook: whenever a webhook integration stops
   receiving events right after a deploy, check what that deploy changed
   before assuming a vendor-side outage. The deploy log is the fastest
   signal, faster than checking a vendor status page.
5. Review whether any other shared secret in the system has the same
   ordering hazard as the billing webhook secret. The support-ticket import
   webhook was flagged as a candidate for the same review, but has not been
   checked yet as of this writing.

## Communication sent to affected customers

A short status update was sent to the handful of customers who had opened
a support ticket asking why an invoice looked unpaid. No proactive mass
email was sent to every affected workspace, since no payment was actually
lost and the dashboard corrected itself automatically once the backlog
drained; this was a deliberate choice to avoid alarming customers over an
issue that had already resolved itself by the time most of them would have
read the email.

## Cost of the incident

No financial loss was recorded: every invoice eventually settled correctly
once the webhook queue drained. The only cost was the 47 minutes of
engineering time from the on-call engineer plus roughly two hours writing
this postmortem and the associated follow-up tickets.

title: 事后分析:三月数据库连接池耗尽事故
content:
三月十二日,亚太区用户在当地时间凌晨报告Coralis Desk仪表盘加载缓慢,部分发票状态长时间停留在待处理。值班的亚太运维同事最先注意到问题,因为影响主要发生在亚洲时段的高峰期,欧洲团队当时还没上线。

排查后发现根因是数据库连接池被耗尽:当天上午的一次批量导入任务打开了大量长连接却没有正确释放,导致后续正常请求排队等待连接,超时后被应用层重试,进一步加剧了连接池压力,形成恶性循环。

处理过程:运维同事先手动重启了导入任务对应的服务,连接数迅速下降,仪表盘在约十五分钟后恢复正常。随后团队为该导入任务加上了连接数上限和超时保护,避免同类任务再次占满连接池。

需要说明的是,这次事故和八月的账单webhook故障表面症状相似(发票停留在待处理状态),但根本原因完全不同,八月那次是签名密钥轮换顺序错误导致webhook被拒绝,和本次的数据库连接池问题没有任何关联,排查时不要把两者混为一谈。

title: Checklist d'onboarding - développeur
content:
Première semaine d'un nouveau développeur chez Coralis :

1. Compte GitHub ajouté à l'organisation, accès au dépôt `coralis-desk`
   accordé en lecture-écriture.
2. Installation de l'environnement local via le script `make dev`, qui
   dépend de Homebrew sur macOS pour installer Go, pnpm et PostgreSQL.
3. Accès au canal Slack `#ingénierie` et `#alerts-prod` (lecture seule les
   deux premières semaines, écriture ensuite).
4. Lecture obligatoire des conventions de code (note dédiée) avant la
   première pull request.
5. Binôme assigné pour les deux premières semaines, revue systématique de
   chaque pull request par ce binôme.
6. Pas d'accès à la production avant la fin du premier mois : les accès
   au bastion et au groupe `deploy-prod` sont demandes explicitement par le
   responsable ops après validation de la période d'intégration.

Le matériel (laptop, écran) est commandé via le formulaire achats standard,
en général deux semaines avant la date d'arrivée pour tenir compte des
délais fournisseur.

title: Checklist d'onboarding - agent support
content:
Première semaine d'un nouvel agent support chez Coralis :

1. Accès à l'outil de tickets interne, avec un quota réduit de tickets
   assignés pendant les deux premières semaines.
2. Lecture des macros de réponse standard : réinitialisation de mot de
   passé, déblocage de compte verrouillé, et politique d'escalade des
   tickets (notes dédiées).
3. Ombrage (shadowing) d'un agent senior pendant trois jours avant de
   prendre ses propres tickets.
4. Accès au canal Slack `#support` en lecture-écriture dès le premier jour,
   contrairement aux développeurs qui n'ont qu'un accès lecture au départ.
5. Formation d'une demi-journee sur les niveaux de SLA et sur les critères
   d'escalade vers l'équipe ingénierie.
6. Aucun accès direct à la base de données de production : toute
   vérification technique passe par l'outil d'administration interne, pas
   par une requête SQL directe.

Contrairement à l'onboarding développeur, il n'y a pas de période d'un mois
avant d'avoir des responsabilités : un agent support traité ses premiers
tickets réels dès la deuxième semaine, sous supervision.

title: Coralis Desk API v2 - versioning and migration guide
content:
## Overview

Coralis Desk's public API is currently on major version 2, latest release
`v2.14.3`. This document explains how versioning works and what changed
since v1.

## Versioning scheme

We follow semver strictly for the public API. Breaking changes only happen
on a major version bump, which historically has happened once every twelve
to eighteen months. Minor and patch releases are always backward
compatible.

## What changed in v2

- Pagination moved from offset-based to cursor-based for every list
  endpoint.
- Webhook payloads now include a `schema_version` field so consumers can
  detect format changes without guessing from the API version alone.
- Rate limits moved from per-API-key to per-workspace, which matters for
  customers who share one key across several integrations.

## Migrating from v1

Customers still on v1 should read the deprecation note (separate document)
for the exact sunset date. In short: v1 stops receiving bug fixes now and
will be shut down entirely on the announced date. There is no automatic
migration; integrations must switch their base URL and adapt to
cursor-based pagination manually.

## Changelog highlights for the 2.14.x line

- `v2.14.0`: added bulk issue import endpoint.
- `v2.14.1`: fixed a pagination cursor that could repeat the last item of a
  page under high write concurrency.
- `v2.14.2`: internal only, no customer-visible change.
- `v2.14.3`: fixed an issue where the `assignee_type` field could be
  returned as `null` instead of the expected enum value when an agent was
  removed from a workspace while still assigned to open issues. This is the
  current recommended version for all new integrations.

## Authentication

API keys are scoped to a single workspace. There is no cross-workspace key.
Rotate keys from the workspace settings page; the old key keeps working for
five minutes after rotation to avoid a hard cutover for long-running jobs.

## Where to report problems

Integration issues should be filed as support tickets, not GitHub issues,
since the public API repository only contains generated client SDKs and no
server code. Include the exact API version you called against and, if
relevant, the ticket number of any related billing or webhook issue so
support can cross-reference it.

## A note on the frontend versus backend split

This document only covers the public HTTP API. Internal coding conventions
for the Go backend and the TypeScript frontend are documented separately
and are not part of the public API contract; changing an internal function
signature does not require a version bump here unless it changes the HTTP
contract.

## Deprecation policy going forward

Starting with v2, any field or endpoint marked deprecated in the changelog
stays functional for at least twelve months before removal, and removal
only happens on a major version bump, never in a minor or patch release.
This is a stricter guarantee than v1 ever had, where fields could
disappear without much warning.

## Rate limit details

Per-workspace rate limits are enforced with a sliding window, not a fixed
per-minute bucket, so a burst right at the boundary of two minutes cannot
double the effective limit the way a fixed window would allow. The exact
numeric limits differ by pricing tier and are documented in the pricing
decision record rather than here, since they are a commercial parameter
that can change independently of the API's technical behavior.

## Webhook delivery guarantees

Webhooks are delivered at-least-once, never exactly-once. Consumers must
be idempotent, using the event identifier included in every payload to
detect and ignore duplicates. Delivery is retried with exponential backoff
for up to 24 hours if the consumer's endpoint returns a non-2xx response or
times out; after 24 hours the event is dropped and only available through
the reconciliation API as a fallback.

## SDKs

Generated client SDKs exist for a handful of languages and are published
from the same repository as this documentation, kept in sync automatically
whenever a new API version ships. Hand-written SDK code is not accepted;
any manual fix should go into the generator instead so it survives the
next regeneration.

## Support for older minor versions within v2

Only the latest patch release of the current minor version and the
previous minor version receive bug fixes. Anything older than that is
expected to upgrade; support will point customers still running an old
2.x minor version at the changelog to identify what changed before helping
debug an issue that a newer patch might already fix.

title: Coralis Desk API v1 - deprecation notice
content:
API v1 was the original public API, launched before Coralis Desk had any
concept of workspaces; every API key mapped to a single account instead.
It used offset-based pagination and did not support webhooks at all,
customers had to poll for changes.

v1 entered deprecation on January 15th 2026 and stopped receiving bug fixes
from that date. The sunset date (full shutdown, all v1 endpoints returning
410 Gone) is set six months later. Any integration still calling v1 after
that date will fail entirely with no fallback.

There is no automated migration tool. Customers must rewrite their
integration against v2, in particular adapting to cursor-based pagination
and to the new workspace-scoped API keys. Support has a migration guide
they can send on request, but engineering will not extend the v1 sunset
date for individual customers.

title: Billing webhook integration - PayLoop (current)
content:
## Overview

Coralis Desk bills customers through PayLoop. PayLoop sends signed webhook
events for every invoice state change, and our webhook consumer verifies
the signature before processing anything.

## Required environment variables

- `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME` - the name of the secret (in our secret
  manager) holding the current signing secret shared with PayLoop. Never
  the secret value itself, only its name; the value is fetched at runtime.
- `BILLING_WEBHOOK_ENDPOINT_PATH` - the path PayLoop posts to, currently
  `/webhooks/payloop`.
- `PAYLOOP_API_KEY_NAME` - name of the secret holding the API key used to
  query PayLoop's REST API for reconciliation.

## Verifying a webhook

```bash
# compute the expected signature and compare it to the header PayLoop sent
# never log the raw secret value, only whether verification passed
secret=$(read_secret "$BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME")
expected=$(echo -n "$payload" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$secret")
# reject anything that does not match, do not process partially-verified events
if [ "$expected" != "$received_signature" ]; then
  echo "signature mismatch, dropping event"
  exit 1
fi
```

## Rotating the signing secret

This is the step that caused the August outage (see the postmortem). The
order matters:

1. Generate the new secret value in PayLoop's dashboard, but do not
   activate it yet on their side.
2. Update the secret in our secret manager under the name held by
   `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME`, and deploy so the new value is picked up.
3. Only then, activate the new secret on PayLoop's side. There is a short
   window where both the old and new secret are accepted on our side to
   avoid a hard cutover.
4. Confirm at least one real webhook has been verified successfully with
   the new secret before removing the old one from the accepted list.

## Reconciliation job

A nightly job calls PayLoop's REST API (using `PAYLOOP_API_KEY_NAME`) to
compare our local invoice states against PayLoop's records, in case any
webhook was missed despite retries. Discrepancies open a support ticket
automatically under the `facturation` label.

## Migrating away from QuickPay

Coralis Desk used to bill through QuickPay before switching to PayLoop.
That integration is documented separately and marked obsolete; it must not
be reactivated, the QuickPay contract was terminated.

## Idempotency and duplicate events

PayLoop can deliver the same event more than once, especially if our
endpoint is slow to respond. Every processed event identifier is recorded
so a duplicate delivery is recognized and skipped rather than double-
applied to an invoice's state. This matters most for the "invoice paid"
event, since applying it twice must never result in a customer being
charged or credited twice on our side.

## Monitoring dashboards

Two dashboards matter for this integration day to day: one tracking
webhook queue depth and processing latency, and one tracking the daily
reconciliation job's discrepancy count. A discrepancy count above zero is
not automatically an incident; a handful of discrepancies per week are
expected and usually self-resolve once a delayed webhook eventually
arrives. Sustained growth in discrepancies over several days, on the other
hand, usually means something is wrong with delivery or with the
reconciliation job itself.

## Sandbox testing

PayLoop provides a sandbox environment with its own separate signing
secret, tracked under a different secret name than production. Never point
the production `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET_NAME` value at the sandbox secret or
vice versa; the two environments must stay fully isolated from each other,
including during manual testing.

## Who to contact at PayLoop

For anything beyond a routine reconciliation discrepancy, escalate through
PayLoop's dedicated integration support address rather than their generic
support form, since the generic form routes to a queue with a much longer
response time than the integration-specific channel that Coralis has
access to as a paying customer on their business plan.

title: Billing webhook integration - QuickPay (obsolete)
content:
Before PayLoop, Coralis Desk billed customers through QuickPay. QuickPay's
webhooks were not signed at all; verification relied on an allowlist of
QuickPay's outbound IP ranges, which QuickPay changed without much notice
on at least two occasions, causing missed events.

The environment variables used at the time were `QUICKPAY_WEBHOOK_TOKEN`
and `QUICKPAY_ALLOWED_IPS`. Neither of these exist anymore in any running
environment; they were removed when the QuickPay contract was terminated
and the PayLoop integration went live.

This document is kept only so that anyone reading old support tickets or
old incident reports from before the migration understands what those
variable names referred to. Do not reintroduce this integration or reuse
these variable names for anything else.

title: Backend coding conventions (Go)
content:
## Scope

These conventions apply to the Go backend of Coralis Desk. They exist
because reviewers were repeatedly flagging the same issues in pull
requests; codifying them here means the checklist is applied consistently
instead of depending on who happens to review.

## Naming

- Package names are short, lowercase, no underscores.
- Exported functions that touch the database live in a `store` or `repo`
  suffix package, never directly in the handler package.
- Error variables are named `Err<Something>` and declared with
  `errors.New` or `fmt.Errorf` with `%w` for wrapping, never a bare string
  comparison.

## Error handling

Errors are never silently swallowed. A function that can fail returns an
error; the caller either handles it explicitly or wraps and propagates it.
`_ = someCall()` to discard an error is only acceptable for a small,
explicitly documented allowlist (closing a response body after logging,
for instance), never for anything that touches persistence or money.

## UUID handling in handlers

Resource path parameters that could be either a UUID or a human-readable
identifier must go through a loader function before being used in a write
query. Trusted UUIDs coming back from generated database code can use the
panicking parse helper, since a malformed value there indicates a bug in
our own code rather than untrusted input.

## Testing

Database-backed tests build their fixtures through the shared test
fixture helpers rather than hand-writing an insert and a matching cleanup
statement in every test. This was not always the convention; a lot of
early tests in this codebase predate the shared helpers and have not all
been migrated, so do not copy patterns from very old test files.

## SQL and migrations

Every new index is created concurrently, in its own migration file, never
inside a transaction with other statements. Foreign keys are not used;
relationships and cleanup are handled explicitly in application code
instead, with an application-level transaction when an operation and its
cleanup must succeed or fail together.

## Formatting and linting

`gofmt` and `go vet` are run before every commit; there is no style
argument to be had beyond what those tools already enforce. Reviewers
should spend their time on logic and naming, not on spacing.

## Late note on comments

Code comments are always written in English, even though a large share of
day-to-day conversation among the team happens in French. This keeps the
codebase readable for the whole engineering team, including newer hires who
may not read French yet.

## Dependency injection and package boundaries

Packages that hold shared business logic must not import anything specific
to a single delivery platform: no direct dependency on a web framework, no
direct filesystem access assuming a particular deployment target.
Anything platform-specific is injected from the outermost layer instead,
so the same business logic package can run in more than one binary without
modification.

## Concurrency

Goroutines started for background work must have an explicit way to be
stopped or to report a panic upward; a goroutine that can silently die
without anyone noticing is treated as a bug during review, not an
acceptable shortcut, even for something that looks like a "fire and
forget" background task.

## Logging conventions

Log lines never include secret values, full request bodies for endpoints
that carry sensitive data, or raw personal data beyond what is strictly
needed to debug an issue. A log line that would leak a signing secret or a
customer's full billing details is treated the same severity as a security
bug in review, not as a minor nitpick.

## Reviewing pull requests

A reviewer is expected to actually run the diff's tests locally when the
change touches anything database-related, not just read the diff. This
slows down review slightly but has caught several bugs that passed CI by
accident due to test ordering or shared fixture state.

## When to open a new package versus adding to an existing one

A new package is justified when the code represents a genuinely separate
concern with its own tests and its own reason to change independently of
its neighbors. Splitting a package purely to make file sizes smaller,
without a real boundary behind the split, is discouraged and comes up
often enough in review to be worth writing down here explicitly.

title: Frontend coding conventions (TypeScript/React)
content:
Coralis Desk's frontend is TypeScript with strict mode enabled everywhere;
avoiding `any` is not optional, a genuinely unknown shape should be typed
as `unknown` and narrowed explicitly.

Server state (anything fetched from the API) and client state (filters,
drafts, open modals) are kept in separate systems rather than mixed in one
global store, so a component never has to guess which one it is reading
from. Components that render the same thing on two different apps get
extracted into the shared views package instead of being copy-pasted, which
was a recurring review comment before this rule was written down.

Network responses are always parsed through a schema before being trusted
as a typed object; casting raw JSON straight to a TypeScript type is
treated as a bug during review, not a style preference, because backend
responses can drift out from under an older installed client.

Optimistic UI updates are reserved for changes that are locally predictable
and rarely fail, like toggling a status; anything that navigates the user
away or deletes something must wait for the server to confirm first.

title: Decision record: new pricing tiers
content:
## Decision

Coralis Desk moves from a single flat per-seat price to three tiers
(Starter, Team, Scale) starting with all new customers signing after the
Q4 roadmap meeting where this was approved.

## Context

The flat per-seat price undercharged large workspaces that used almost no
support-agent seats but heavy API usage, and overcharged small teams that
wanted agent assignees but only a handful of human seats. Several churned
customers cited pricing rigidity in exit interviews conducted by the
support team.

## Options considered

1. Keep flat per-seat pricing, just raise the price. Rejected: does not fix
   the underlying mismatch between usage pattern and price, it only delays
   the same complaints.
2. Pure usage-based pricing (API calls, storage). Rejected: too
   unpredictable for finance teams who need to budget in advance, based on
   feedback gathered directly from several enterprise prospects.
3. Three tiers combining a seat allowance with API call limits. Chosen.

## The three tiers

- Starter: up to 5 human seats, unlimited agent assignees, a modest monthly
  API call allowance, intended for very small teams.
- Team: up to 25 human seats, higher API allowance, includes the hybrid
  Brain search feature at no extra cost.
- Scale: unlimited seats, custom API allowance negotiated per contract,
  dedicated support channel.

## Grandfathering existing customers

Every customer who signed before the new tiers went live keeps their old
flat per-seat price indefinitely, as long as they do not request a plan
change themselves. If they explicitly ask to move to a new tier, they
cannot go back to the old flat pricing afterward; this is a one-way switch,
and support should say this explicitly before making the change on a
customer's request.

## What this does not change

Existing billing infrastructure (PayLoop integration, invoice webhooks) is
unaffected; only the price calculation logic changes, not the payment
rails. Support ticket escalation for billing disputes still follows the
existing SLA levels regardless of tier.

## Rollout

New tiers are live for new signups immediately after this decision;
existing customers are notified by email about the grandfathering policy
but nothing changes for them unless they act.

## Impact on the sales process

Sales conversations now start by understanding a prospect's expected human-
seat count and API usage pattern before quoting a tier, instead of quoting
a flat per-seat number from memory. This adds a short discovery step to
every sales call that did not exist before, which the sales team flagged
as a minor friction but accepted as worthwhile given the churn reasons
described above.

## Handling mid-cycle upgrades

A customer who upgrades from Starter to Team mid-billing-cycle is charged
a prorated difference for the remainder of the current cycle, then the full
Team price from the next cycle onward. Downgrades take effect only at the
next renewal, never immediately, to avoid mid-cycle refund complexity that
the finance team specifically asked to avoid when this decision was drafted.

## Interaction with the mobile app decision

Because Team and Scale tiers are the ones most likely to ask about a
native mobile app, the pricing decision explicitly notes that entitlement
language for tiers should be written in a way that does not promise a
native app feature that does not exist yet, given the separate decision to
not build one this year.

## Metrics to watch after rollout

The team agreed to track, for three months after rollout, the distribution
of new signups across the three tiers and the rate of tier changes among
existing customers who voluntarily opt into the new structure. If Starter
sign-ups turn out unexpectedly high relative to Team, that would suggest
the tier boundaries need revisiting at the next roadmap meeting, though no
such revisit has been scheduled yet as of this decision.

## What triggered this decision

This decision was not proposed in isolation; it followed directly from the
roadmap discussion recorded in the Q3 and Q4 meeting notes, where pricing
rigidity was flagged as an open point carried over from Q3 into Q4 and
resolved with this record.

title: Décision: pas d'application mobile native cette année
content:
Décision actée en réunion roadmap T3 puis reconfirmée en T4 : Coralis ne lance pas d'application mobile native cette année, malgré plusieurs
demandes clients récurrentes sur ce sujet dans les retours support.

Raisons principales : l'équipe ingénierie est déjà engagée sur le chantier
de recherche hybride dans le Brain, jugée prioritaire, et une application
mobile native représenterait un chantier séparé avec sa propre pile
technique, ses propres cycles de publication sur les stores, et sa propre
charge de maintenance continue.

Alternative retenue en attendant : améliorer la version web mobile
(navigateur) pour qu'elle couvre les usages les plus fréquents en
déplacement (consultation de tickets, changement de statut), sans viser la
parité complète avec la version bureau.

Cette décision sera revue à la prochaine réunion roadmap si le volume de
demandes clients continue d'augmenter significativement, mais aucune date
de réévaluation n'est fixée pour l'instant au-dela du cycle trimestriel
habituel.

title: Runbook: production database restore
content:
## When to use this runbook

Use this only for a real data-loss incident or a scheduled disaster
recovery drill, never to "quickly check" something in production data.
Restoring pulls a snapshot into an isolated instance; it never touches the
live database directly.

## Prerequisites

- Access to the backup storage bucket (read-only role is enough for a
  restore, do not request write access for this task).
- The exact timestamp or backup identifier you need to restore, confirmed
  with whoever requested the restore.
- A dedicated restore instance provisioned ahead of time, never restore
  onto an instance that also serves other traffic.

## Restoring the latest full backup

```bash
# list available backups, newest first
list_backups --newest-first
# download the chosen backup to the restore instance
fetch_backup --id="$BACKUP_ID" --dest=/mnt/restore
# restore into a fresh, isolated database, never the live one
restore_db --from=/mnt/restore --target=restore-instance
```

## Point-in-time recovery

For an incident where we need the database state at an exact moment (for
example, right before a bad migration ran), point-in-time recovery replays
the write-ahead log on top of the nearest full backup up to the requested
timestamp.

```bash
# replay WAL segments up to (but not including) the bad migration commit
restore_db --from=/mnt/restore --target=restore-instance \
  --point-in-time="2026-08-19T13:58:00Z"
# verify row counts on a few known tables before trusting the restore
verify_restore --target=restore-instance --tables=issues,workspaces
```

Point-in-time recovery is the slower path and should only be used when a
full backup restore is not precise enough for the incident, because replaying
the log can take significantly longer than restoring a full snapshot,
depending on how much write-ahead log has accumulated since the last
backup.

## Handing off to the requester

Once the restore instance is verified, hand off the connection details to
whoever requested the restore; do not run any application code against the
restore instance yourself unless explicitly asked, since query patterns can
differ from what a human reviewer expects when comparing data.

## After the drill or incident

Tear down the restore instance once it is no longer needed. It should never
be left running as a permanent second database, and it should never receive
production traffic under any circumstance.

## Backup retention

Full backups are retained for 35 days on a rolling basis; write-ahead log
segments needed for point-in-time recovery are retained for the same
window. Anything older than that is not recoverable through this runbook
at all, there is no cold-storage tier beyond the 35-day window as of this
writing.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Restoring directly onto the primary instance instead of an isolated
  restore instance. There is no legitimate reason to ever do this.
- Forgetting to verify row counts before handing off the restore instance,
  which has led in the past to a requester assuming a restore was complete
  when it had actually stalled partway through replay.
- Using a backup identifier from memory instead of listing available
  backups first; backup identifiers are not sequential and guessing one
  can silently restore the wrong point in time.

## Testing this runbook

This runbook is exercised at least twice a year through a scheduled drill,
independent of the annual security incident simulation exercise described
in the security incident response plan; the two exercises are unrelated
and test different failure modes; do not treat completing one as
satisfying the requirement for the other.

## Escalation if the restore itself fails

If the restore command fails partway through, do not retry blindly more
than once. A second failure with the same backup identifier usually means
the backup itself is corrupted rather than a transient issue, and should
be escalated immediately to whoever owns the backup pipeline rather than
retried repeatedly, since repeated retries against a corrupted backup
mostly waste time during an already stressful incident.

## Relationship to the March incident

The March database connection-pool incident did not require a restore;
restarting the affected service was enough to release the exhausted
connections. This runbook exists for genuine data-loss scenarios, which is
a different class of problem than a resource-exhaustion incident, even
though both are database-related.

title: Runbook - renouvellement du certificat SSL
content:
Le certificat SSL de l'API de production est configuré dans
`/etc/nginx/conf.d/api.conf` et renouvelé automatiquement via un job
planifié qui tourne toutes les nuits, largement avant l'échéance réelle.

En cas d'échec du renouvellement automatique (alerte spécifique sur le
canal Slack `#alerts-prod`), la procédure manuelle consiste à relancer le
client de renouvellement, vérifier que le nouveau certificat est bien pris
en compte par nginx sans redémarrage complet du service (rechargement à chaud uniquement), puis contrôler depuis l'extérieur que la date
d'expiration affichée correspond au nouveau certificat.

Ne jamais modifier `/etc/nginx/conf.d/api.conf` à la main en production
sans passer par la procédure de déploiement standard : ce fichier est
régénéré automatiquement à chaque renouvellement et toute modification
manuelle non versionnée serait perdue au renouvellement suivant.

Une échéance de renouvellement manquée sans intervention entraînerait une
coupure totale de l'API en HTTPS pour tous les clients, ce qui en fait une
alerte à traiter en priorité absolue, avant même les alertes de latence.

title: Plan de réponse a un incident de sécurité
content:
## Objectif

Ce document décrit la procédure à suivre en cas de suspicion d'incident de
sécurité touchant Coralis Desk : accès non autorisé, fuite de données
suspectée, ou compromission d'un compte à privilèges élevés.

## Détection et première alerte

Toute personne de l'équipe qui suspecte un incident de sécurité doit le
signaler immédiatement sur le canal Slack dédié à la sécurité, même en cas
de doute : il est préférable de lever une fausse alerte que de retarder un
signalement réel.

## Confinement immédiat

Les premières actions visent à limiter la propagation, pas à comprendre la
cause complète : révocation immédiate des accès suspectés, rotation des
secrets potentiellement exposés, et isolation des systèmes concernés si
nécessaire. Ces actions ne doivent pas attendre une analyse complète.

## Qualification de la gravité

Une fois le confinement effectue, l'équipe qualifie la gravité de
l'incident selon trois niveaux : mineur (aucune donnée client concernée),
majeur (accès non autorisé sans exfiltration confirmée), critique
(exfiltration de données personnelles confirmée ou très probable).

## Communication interne

Pour un incident qualifié majeur ou critique, la direction est informée
sans délai, avant même la fin de l'investigation technique complète.

## Notification externe et obligations réglementaires

Pour un incident critique impliquant des données personnelles de clients
européens, la notification à la CNIL doit intervenir dans un délai de
soixante-douze heures à compter de la connaissance de l'incident, même si
l'investigation n'est pas terminée : une notification initiale incomplète
suivie d'un complément est préférable à une notification tardive. Le
responsable juridique (voir le contact du cabinet partenaire) est associé à la rédaction de cette notification.

Les clients concernés sont notifiés individuellement si leurs données
personnelles sont impliquées, avec un délai qui dépend de la nature exacte
des données, mais qui ne doit jamais dépasser celui imposé par la
réglementation applicable.

## Post-incident

Un rapport post-incident est rédigé dans les deux semaines suivant la
résolution, sur le même modèle que les postmortems techniques, mais avec
une section supplémentaire dédiée aux obligations réglementaires
effectivement remplies et à leurs dates.

## Rôles et responsabilités pendant l'incident

Un incident de sécurité désigne systématiquement une seule personne comme
coordinatrice de l'incident, distincte de la personne qui a détecté le
problème. Cette coordination évite que plusieurs personnes prennent des
décisions contradictoires en même temps, par exemple révoquer un accès
d'un côté pendant qu'une autre personne tente de s'y reconnecter de
l'autre pour investiguer.

## Conservation des preuves

Avant toute action de confinement qui modifierait l'état d'un système
(révocation d'accès, redémarrage), les journaux et états pertinents
doivent être copiées dans un espace de stockage prévu à cet effet, dans la mesure où cela ne retarde pas significativement le confinement lui-même. Un
confinement qui sauve des données clients passe toujours avant la
conservation parfaite des preuves, mais on ne détruit jamais une preuve
sans nécessité.

## Astreinte sécurité spécifique

Contrairement à l'astreinte technique générale décrite dans la procédure
de déploiement, l'astreinte sécurité suit un planning distinct et plus
restreint : seules les personnes ayant suivi la formation interne
dédiée peuvent être d'astreinte sécurité. Le contact de cette astreinte
est différent du contact de l'astreinte ops habituelle et ne doit pas être
confondu avec lui en cas d'urgence.

## Exercices de simulation

Un exercice de simulation d'incident de sécurité est organisé au moins une
fois par an, avec un scénario différent chaque année, pour vérifier que la
procédure décrite ici reste comprise et applicable par l'équipe, et pas
seulement lue une fois à l'onboarding puis oubliée.

## Lien avec la revue trimestrielle des accès

La revue trimestrielle des accès (voir la note dédiée) n'est pas une
procédure de réponse à un incident, mais les écarts qu'elle détecte
(permissions non révoquées, comptes inactifs toujours actifs) sont une
source fréquente de vulnérabilités qui peuvent, si elles sont exploitées,
déclencher exactement le type d'incident décrit dans ce document.

title: 季度访问权限审查流程
content:
每个季度末,IT团队对所有生产环境访问权限进行一次系统性审查,目的是发现并移除不再需要的权限,而不是等到安全事件发生后才补救。

审查范围包括堡垒机SSH访问权限、deploy-prod用户组成员、数据库只读和读写角色分配,以及第三方服务(如账单供应商PayLoop的管理后台)的账号列表。任何离职员工的权限必须在离职当天之内撤销,这一点不属于季度审查的范畴,而是入职离职流程本身就要保证的最低要求。

季度审查重点关注的是"权限累积"问题:员工换岗或参与临时项目后被授予的权限,如果没有人主动撤销,会一直保留下去。审查时由各团队负责人逐条确认名下成员是否仍然需要对应权限,凡是负责人在两周内未回复确认的权限,默认视为可以撤销,而不是默认保留。

审查结果和撤销记录归档保存,作为安全事件响应流程中回溯"谁在什么时间有什么权限"的重要依据。

title: Politique de télétravail
content:
Coralis fonctionne en mode hybride : deux jours de présence au bureau
minimum par semaine pour les équipes basées en France, le reste en
télétravail au choix de chacun, sous réserve de coordination avec son
équipe pour les jours de présence communs.

Le télétravail depuis l'étranger est possible ponctuellement (jusqu'à
quatre semaines par an) mais doit être déclaré à l'avance aux RH pour des
raisons fiscales et de couverture sociale, pas seulement par courtoisie.

L'entreprise fournit un forfait d'équipement pour le domicile (écran,
chaise) une fois par période de trois ans, commandé via le même formulaire
achats que le matériel de bureau.

Les réunions d'équipe importantes (revues de roadmap, entretiens annuels)
restent en présentiel dans la mesure du possible, même pour les personnes
qui travaillent habituellement à distance la plupart du temps.

title: 报销政策
content:
员工因公产生的费用可通过内部报销系统提交,需要在费用发生后三十天内提交,超过三十天的报销申请默认不予受理,除非有部门负责人特批的书面说明。

常见可报销项目包括:客户拜访交通费、团队建设活动费用、异地出差住宿(需提前通过内部审批,不能先订后补批)、以及经批准的培训课程费用。办公用品和日常耗材不走员工报销流程,统一通过采购部门下单。

报销单必须附带正规发票或收据原件的扫描件,没有票据的费用一律不予报销,口头说明或聊天记录截图都不能替代票据。超过一定金额的报销单(具体金额线由财务负责人在入职培训中说明)需要额外经过部门负责人和财务负责人双重审批才能放款。

报销款项一般在提交并审批通过后的下一个发薪周期内随工资一起发放,不单独打款。

title: 亚太支持团队月度会议记录
content:
## 会议概况

本月亚太支持团队会议由团队全员参加,主要议题包括上月工单回顾、当前积压情况,以及即将到来的中国法定节假日期间的值班安排。

## 上月工单回顾

上月总工单量比前一个月略有上升,主要集中在账单相关问题和登录问题两大类。其中有一张工单(编号SUP-1042)被多次提及,客户反馈发票列表页面在数据量较大的工作区加载明显变慢,后续排查发现与数据库索引有关,详情记录在另一份专门的技术笔记中,这里不重复展开。

## 积压情况

截至会议当天,待处理工单积压量处于可接受范围内,平均首次响应时间符合当前SLA等级的要求。有两名新加入的支持同事仍在轮岗观察期,他们的工单量按照入职清单里的规定被人为限制,不计入积压压力的评估。

## 节假日值班安排

即将到来的中国法定节假日期间,亚太支持团队按照往年惯例安排轮值,保证核心时段(当地上午九点到下午六点)至少有一名支持同事在线处理紧急工单,非紧急工单可以延后到假期结束后处理,不需要在假期内强行清零积压。具体轮值表已经在团队内部单独同步,不在本会议记录中列出姓名。

## 与欧洲团队的协作提醒

会议最后特别提醒:凡是需要升级到工程团队的工单,升级标准和SLA等级请参照支持工单升级政策这份文档,不要凭经验自行判断是否需要升级,尤其是涉及账单webhook或数据库性能相关的工单,应该优先升级而不是自行长时间排查。

## 下次会议

下次月度会议维持相同形式:上月回顾加下月关注点,时间待定,由团队负责人在群里另行通知。

## 客户反馈汇总

除了工单数据本身,本次会议还汇总了几条比较有代表性的客户反馈,供产品团队参考。有客户提到希望发票列表页面支持按到期日排序后仍然保持较快的加载速度,这一点和SUP-1042那张工单反映的问题基本一致,说明该问题的影响面比最初以为的更广,不止一个工作区受影响。另有客户反馈,登录失败次数过多后账号被锁定的机制没有明确提示还剩几次尝试机会,建议在提示文案上做优化,这条反馈已经记录并会转达给产品团队,但本次会议不做进一步处理。

## 值班同事的常见困惑

新加入轮岗观察期的两名同事在会议上提出了几个共同的困惑,团队负责人当场做了澄清:第一,重置密码和解锁账号是两个不同的操作入口,不能用同一个按钮处理,详见对应的支持宏文档;第二,遇到账单相关的异常,不要自己在数据库层面查,统一通过内部管理工具查看,这一点在支持团队入职清单里已经写明,但新同事容易忘记;第三,升级工单给工程团队之前,需要按照支持工单升级政策里的标准先确认基本信息,不能只写一句笼统的描述就转过去。

## 跨团队沟通渠道回顾

会议专门回顾了一次跨团队沟通不畅的情况:上个月一张涉及数据库性能的工单在支持团队内部排查了将近一天才升级,超过了升级政策里规定的三十分钟标准,原因是当时值班同事以为这只是普通的页面卡顿,没有意识到符合"必须升级"的条件。团队负责人重申:遇到不确定要不要升级的情况,原则上倾向于升级,不要因为担心打扰工程团队而拖延,升级之后如果证明确实是小问题,也远好于拖延导致客户等待过久。

## 值班表说明

本次会议确认的值班安排只覆盖即将到来的法定节假日期间,平时的值班表是每周单独发布的,和本次讨论的假期值班表是两份不同的文档,不要把两者混在一起查阅,以免看错日期导致值班空缺。

## 会议纪要归档

本次会议纪要和历史上每个月的会议纪要一样,归档在团队共享空间中,方便日后追溯某个月的工单量、客户反馈或值班安排,归档本身不需要额外操作,会议结束后由记录员直接保存即可。

title: 上海办公室新员工入职清单
content:
上海办公室新员工入职当天需要完成以下事项:签署劳动合同并留存人事部门存档一份;开通公司邮箱和内部协作工具账号;领取工位相关设备(电脑、屏幕),设备申领同样走公司统一的采购表单流程,和法国办公室使用同一套流程,只是审批人不同。

第一周需要完成:阅读并确认已知悉休假政策和报销政策两份文档(内容各自独立,不要混淆两份文档里的天数和金额限制);如果是技术岗位,还需要额外完成开发者入职清单中列出的账号和环境配置事项;如果是支持岗位,则完成支持团队入职清单中列出的工单系统权限开通和跟岗安排。

试用期一般为三个月,期间由直属负责人安排每两周一次的沟通,试用期结束前两周由负责人提交评估意见给人事部门,而不是等试用期最后一天才提交。

title: Investigation note: slow invoice list queries
content:
Support ticket `SUP-1042` reported that the invoice list page was loading
noticeably slowly for workspaces with a large invoice history, sometimes
taking several seconds instead of the usual sub-second response.

Investigation traced the slowness to a full table scan on the invoices
table whenever the list was filtered and sorted by due date, which is the
default sort order on that page. There was no index supporting that access
pattern; the existing indexes only covered lookups by workspace and by
invoice status, not by due date.

The fix was adding `idx_invoice_due_date`, a concurrently-built index
covering workspace, status and due date together, matching exactly the
filter-and-sort pattern the page uses. After the index was added, the same
query dropped from several seconds to well under a hundred milliseconds
for the workspace that originally reported the ticket.

This is purely a read-path performance fix; it did not require any change
to how invoices are written, and it has no relationship to the billing
webhook integration or to PayLoop at all, despite both being under the
`facturation` tag.

title: 支持工单升级政策
content:
支持工单分为三个优先级:普通、紧急、严重。普通工单的首次响应时间标准为一个工作日以内,紧急工单为四小时以内,严重工单要求三十分钟以内响应并立即评估是否需要升级给工程团队。

以下情况必须升级给工程团队,不允许支持同事自行长时间排查:涉及生产环境数据异常(例如账单状态错误、发票金额不对)、涉及疑似安全问题(异常登录、疑似未授权访问)、以及任何客户报告的性能问题在初步排查后无法在三十分钟内定位原因的情况。

升级时需要在工单中附上已经确认过的基本信息(客户工作区标识、问题发生的大致时间、是否可以稳定复现),不要只写一句"客户反馈异常"就直接转给工程团队,这样会拖慢工程团队的排查速度。

升级不等于放弃处理这张工单:支持同事仍然是客户沟通的第一联系人,负责把工程团队的排查进展及时转达给客户,除非工程团队明确说明需要直接联系客户。

title: Internal acronym glossary
content:
A running glossary of acronyms used across Coralis Desk documentation, kept
here because new hires keep asking the same questions in their first weeks.

- SLA: service level agreement, the response-time commitment tied to a
  support ticket's priority level.
- ARR: annual recurring revenue, tracked by finance, not something support
  or engineering need to reference day to day.
- MRR: monthly recurring revenue, same caveat as ARR.
- SUP-xxxx: the numbering scheme for support tickets, referenced in
  engineering investigation notes when a bug was first reported through a
  ticket rather than found internally.
- CDN: content delivery network, relevant to the APAC hosting vendor
  contract but not something engineering configures directly day to day.
- RTO / RPO: recovery time objective and recovery point objective, used in
  the database restore runbook to describe how fast and how fresh a
  restore needs to be.

This glossary is intentionally short; it only covers acronyms that came up
often enough in onboarding to be worth writing down, not an exhaustive
dictionary of every term used anywhere in the company.
